text_blocks.snippet: High blood pressure (hypertension) is defined as a reading that is consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg.
snippet_highlighted_words: a reading that is consistently at or above 130/80 mm Hg

text_blocks.snippet: Blood pressure is measured in millimeters of mercury (mm Hg) using two numbers:

list.snippet: Systolic (top number): The pressure in your arteries when your heart beats.
Diastolic (bottom number): The pressure in your arteries when your heart rests between beats.

text_blocks.snippet: The American Heart Association and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention break down blood pressure into these ranges:

snippet_links.text: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

list.snippet: Normal: Less than 120 mm Hg (systolic) and less than 80 mm Hg (diastolic)
Elevated: 120–129 mm Hg (systolic) and less than 80 mm Hg (diastolic)
Stage 1 Hypertension: 130–139 mm Hg (systolic) or 80–89 mm Hg (diastolic)
Stage 2 Hypertension: 140 mm Hg or higher (systolic) or 90 mm Hg or higher (diastolic)
Severe Hypertension / Hypertensive Crisis: Higher than 180 mm Hg (systolic) and/or higher than 120 mm Hg (diastolic)

text_blocks.snippet: For more detailed health guidance, visit the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute.

snippet_links.text: National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute

list.snippet: Stage 1 or Stage 2: Schedule a visit with your doctor. A single high reading does not mean you have hypertension; doctors look for patterns over multiple readings.
Higher than 180/120 mm Hg (Hypertensive Crisis): Wait 5 minutes and test again. If it is still that high and you have no symptoms, contact your doctor immediately.
Call 911 Immediately: If your reading is higher than 180/120 mm Hg and you experience warning signs like chest pain, shortness of breath, back pain, numbness, weakness, or a change in vision.
